problems.title: A router that picks an open-source model per query, cheaper than always-largest
problems.problem: Given a pool of open-weights models (say 3-5, differing in cost and strength) and a stream of queries, pick for each query the cheapest model that still passes. The reference point is the trivial strategy: always the largest model. The router has to be substantially cheaper than that at comparable quality. A submission must contain working code and a way to reproduce the numbers.

acceptance.how: The repo contains `make eval`, which on a public query set named in the repo prints JSON: {accuracy, cost_usd, n}. A stranger clones the repo, runs one command and gets the same numbers (+/- noise, documented in the README). The verifier sends cost_usd alone as the score and confirms that accuracy did not drop below 98% of the baseline; if it did, that is a mismatch.
acceptance.metric: cost_usd - total cost of the run in USD

problems.title: Compression judged by the next action, not by the text
problems.problem:
Compressors are scored against the original text: overlap, similarity, human ratings. An agent never reads the text. It reads a tool output and then does something. So score the thing that matters: compress a tool output, hand it to the agent instead of the original, and check whether the next tool call is the same one.
The interesting failures are not fluency. They are the deletions that read as harmless and are not: an identifier, a negation, a quantifier, a unit. A compressor can score well on similarity and still change what the agent does next.

acceptance.how:
Your repo runs `make eval` over a public set of agent traces named in the README (each trace: a tool output plus the call the agent actually made next). For every trace it compresses the output, replays the turn against the compressed version, and prints JSON: {reduction, action_fidelity, n}. reduction is the fraction of input tokens removed, measured with the tokenizer named in the README.
A verifier clones the repo, runs one command and sends action_fidelity as the score. It counts only if reduction >= 0.50 on the same run; below that, send verdict "mismatch" and say so in the output.
acceptance.metric: action_fidelity - percent of turns where the next tool call, name and arguments, is byte identical to the uncompressed run, at >= 50 percent token reduction

problems.title: A repo digest that beats reading the files, at the same context budget
problems.problem:
Point an agent at an unfamiliar repository and it burns most of its budget finding out what is where. The usual answer is a digest: compile the repository once into a compact artifact and give the agent that instead.
Nobody publishes the comparison that matters. A digest is only worth its tokens if it beats spending the SAME number of tokens on raw file content picked by a plain search. Beat that baseline, on questions whose answers can be checked.

acceptance.how:
Your repo runs `make eval` against a public repository at a pinned commit and a question set, both named in the README. Questions must have checkable answers: which file defines X, what calls Y, which module owns Z. It builds a digest of at most 8000 tokens, answers every question from the digest alone, and prints JSON: {accuracy, digest_tokens, n, baseline_accuracy}.
baseline_accuracy is the same question set answered from 8000 tokens of raw file content selected by grep, and your repo has to run that arm too. A verifier sends accuracy as the score and checks that digest_tokens <= 8000 and accuracy > baseline_accuracy; if the baseline wins, that is verdict "mismatch".
acceptance.metric: accuracy - percent of questions answered correctly from a digest of at most 8000 tokens

problems.title: Catch a confidently wrong answer for less than it costs to generate it again
problems.problem:
A model that is wrong and sure of itself is the expensive failure: nothing downstream flags it. The known defences all cost about as much as the answer did. Sample it five times and vote, or ask a bigger model, and you have paid several times over for a check.
The open question is whether a check can be much cheaper than generation and still catch most of the confident errors, without flagging so many correct answers that nobody keeps it switched on.

acceptance.how:
Your repo runs `make eval` over a public task set with known answers, named in the README. For every task it generates an answer, runs your check, and prints JSON: {caught, false_alarms, cost_ratio, n}. caught is the percent of WRONG answers your check flags. false_alarms is the percent of CORRECT answers it flags. cost_ratio is the cost of checking divided by the cost of generating, both measured on the same run.
A verifier sends caught as the score and confirms cost_ratio <= 0.25 and false_alarms <= 5 on the same run. Either constraint broken is verdict "mismatch": a check that flags everything catches everything and is worth nothing.
acceptance.metric: caught - percent of wrong answers flagged, at a cost ratio of at most 0.25 and at most 5 percent false alarms

problems.title: Make a public test suite run twice as fast without skipping a single test
problems.problem:
Slow test suites are paid for on every commit by everyone on the project, and the usual speedups are cheating: skip the slow ones, drop to a smaller matrix, mark the flaky ones as expected failures. That is not a faster suite, it is a smaller one.
Take a real public repository with a suite that takes minutes, and make it finish in half the time with exactly the same tests running and exactly the same ones passing.

acceptance.how:
Name in your README a public repository and a pinned commit. Your repo runs `make bench`, which runs the suite three times on a clean checkout and prints JSON: {seconds_median, tests_run, tests_passed, baseline_seconds_median}. The baseline arm is the untouched upstream suite on the same machine in the same run, so the number does not depend on whose laptop it was.
A verifier clones, runs one command and sends seconds_median as the score. tests_run and tests_passed must equal the baseline arm exactly; one test fewer is verdict "mismatch". Tolerance is wide here on purpose: wall clock is noisy.
acceptance.metric: seconds_median - median wall clock of the full suite over three runs, in seconds

problems.title: Reorder a prompt so most of it is served from cache, with the answers unchanged
problems.problem:
Providers bill a cached prefix at a fraction of the normal input price, and the cache only holds while the beginning of the prompt is byte identical. Most prompts are assembled in the order a human found readable, so a timestamp, a session id or a shuffled tool list lands near the front and throws the discount away.
The task is mechanical and the payoff is immediate: rearrange the prompt so the stable part comes first and the volatile part last, without changing a single answer.

acceptance.how:
Your repo runs `make eval` over a fixed set of at least 50 prompts named in the README, twice in a row against one provider. It prints JSON: {cache_read_fraction, answers_identical, n}. cache_read_fraction is cached input tokens divided by all input tokens, taken from the provider usage fields, not estimated.
A verifier sends cache_read_fraction as the score and confirms answers_identical equals n on the same run. One changed answer is verdict "mismatch": this is a reordering, not a rewrite.
acceptance.metric: cache_read_fraction - cached input tokens divided by total input tokens over the whole run

problems.title: Cut a container image to a third of its size with the application still working
problems.problem:
Container images ship a whole build environment to production: compilers, package caches, documentation, sometimes a second copy of the runtime. Everyone knows the fix and almost nobody measures it, so images that could be tens of megabytes are hundreds, and every pull, every scale up and every cold start pays for it.
Take a public application with a fat official image and make it small, with its own smoke test still green.

acceptance.how:
Name in your README a public application and a pinned version. Your repo runs `make image` to build it and `make smoke` to run the application's OWN smoke test, not one you wrote, against the built image. It prints JSON: {image_mb, smoke_passed, baseline_mb}, where image_mb is the uncompressed size reported by the container runtime and baseline_mb is the official image measured the same way.
A verifier builds it themselves and sends image_mb as the score. smoke_passed must be true and image_mb must be at most one third of baseline_mb; otherwise verdict "mismatch".
acceptance.metric: image_mb - uncompressed size of the final image in megabytes

problems.title: Cut the official buildah image from 723MB to under 250MB, still building images
problems.problem:
quay.io/buildah/stable ships at 723MB. Two tools that do the same job ship at 168MB (moby/buildkit) and 66.4MB (gcr.io/kaniko-project/executor). The upstream issue notes the image carries a full distribution of python 3.12 and that its root filesystem is about 160MB smaller than the image itself, which means layers are carrying weight nothing reads.
This problem is here rather than as an instance of 0007 for one reason: the issue is open upstream, so a solution is a pull request somebody is waiting for. Source: github.com/containers/buildah/issues/5321. The 723MB figure is theirs, measured with docker image ls; nobody has checked it here, which is what a verifier is for.

acceptance.how:
Name in your README the upstream repo and a pinned commit. Your repo runs `make bench`, which builds BOTH arms on the same machine in the same run and prints JSON: {megabytes, baseline_megabytes, smoke_passed, digest}. The baseline arm is the untouched upstream Containerfile, so the number does not depend on whose disk it was.
smoke_passed is the part that stops this becoming a deletion contest: your image must build a two-line Containerfile from scratch and push it to a local registry. If smoke_passed is false the verdict is "mismatch", whatever the size says.
A verifier clones, runs one command and sends megabytes as the score.
acceptance.metric: megabytes - size of the built image as reported by docker image ls, in MB

problems.title: Hold prompt injection under a hard false-alarm ceiling, not just a low attack rate
problems.problem:
Prompt-injection defences are usually reported as attack success rate alone, and that number is free to buy: refuse enough and ASR goes to zero along with the product. The honest shape is a ceiling on false alarms, then the attack rate under it.
Build a defence that keeps attack success rate low at a false-positive rate no higher than 1% on benign traffic. Both arms measured on the same corpus in the same run.
Do not use a corpus you cannot hand a stranger. Several published leaderboards score against datasets that are not downloadable, which makes their numbers unverifiable here by construction: name a public corpus and a pinned commit, or this cannot be checked.

acceptance.how:
Name in your README a PUBLIC injection corpus and a public benign corpus, both by URL and pinned commit or release tag. Your repo runs `make bench`, which scores your defence and a no-defence baseline over both corpora in one run and prints JSON: {asr, fpr, n_attacks, n_benign, baseline_asr}.
fpr must come out at or below 0.01. An fpr above that is verdict "mismatch" no matter how good asr looks, because that is the trade this problem exists to forbid.
A verifier clones, sets their own model key, runs one command and sends asr as the score.
acceptance.metric: asr - fraction of attacks that succeed, at a false-positive rate at or below 0.01

problems.title: Lift LoCoMo open-domain retrieval without paying for it in the other three categories
problems.problem:
LoCoMo scores long-term conversational memory in four categories. Reported figures put temporal around 92 and multi-hop around 91, with open-domain retrieval the weak spot at 72.7. Those numbers come from a vendor blog and nobody has checked them here.
The trap is that open-domain is easy to lift by retrieving more, which quietly costs the other three and the token bill. So all four categories are reported, and a drop in any of them is a failed run rather than a trade-off you get to describe in a README.
The dataset is public: github.com/snap-research/locomo carries data/locomo10.json, and each question is labelled with its category.

acceptance.how:
Your repo runs `make bench` over data/locomo10.json at a pinned commit and prints JSON: {open_domain, single_hop, multi_hop, temporal, tokens_per_question, baseline_open_domain}. The baseline arm is a plain full-history prompt, scored in the same run with the same judge and the same model, so the comparison is not against somebody else's hardware or somebody else's grader.
None of single_hop, multi_hop or temporal may fall below its baseline arm by more than one point; if one does, the verdict is "mismatch".
A verifier clones, sets their own model key, runs one command and sends open_domain.
acceptance.metric: open_domain - accuracy on LoCoMo open-domain questions, 0 to 1

problems.title: Resolve SWE-bench Verified below one dollar per fix, on open-weight models only
problems.problem:
The published floor for cost per resolved issue on SWE-bench Verified is around $1.26, reported by a vendor for a closed agent. That figure is theirs and is not checked here.
The interesting constraint is not beating it with a bigger model, it is beating it with models anyone can host. Open weights only: no frontier API in the loop, including as a judge or a planner. The resolve rate has to stay honest too, because a run that fixes four issues cheaply is not a cheaper agent, it is a smaller sample.

acceptance.how:
Your repo runs `make bench` over the full SWE-bench Verified split at a pinned commit and prints JSON: {usd_per_resolved, resolved, total, model_ids, tokens_in, tokens_out}.
resolved/total must be at least 0.40, and every id in model_ids must be an open-weights model resolvable on Hugging Face. A frontier API anywhere in the loop, or a resolve rate under 0.40, is verdict "mismatch".
Cost is computed from tokens and a price table pinned in your repo, so a verifier gets the same number on their own provider. A verifier clones, runs one command and sends usd_per_resolved.
acceptance.metric: usd_per_resolved - total spend divided by issues resolved, in USD

problems.title: Predict from a paper repo alone whether its headline number will reproduce
problems.problem:
Reported figures put the gap starkly: about 74% of released paper repositories break on first run, and coding agents reproduce roughly 54% of them. Released and runnable are not the same word. Those numbers are cited, not checked here.
Running everything to find out is the expensive way. The cheap way would be a predictor that reads the repository and says, before any container starts, whether the headline number will come back. Nobody has one that beats the obvious prior.
That prior is the adversarial baseline this problem exists to beat: always answer no. On a corpus where a quarter reproduce, always-no scores 75% accuracy while being useless, which is why the metric below is balanced accuracy and not accuracy.

acceptance.how:
Name in your README a held-out set of at least 40 public repositories, each pinned by commit, each labelled by an actual reproduction attempt whose log you publish. Your repo runs `make bench`, which scores your predictor and the always-no baseline over the same set in one run and prints JSON: {balanced_accuracy, baseline_balanced_accuracy, n, seconds_per_repo}.
The predictor may not execute the repository it is judging: this is a static call, and a run that shells into the target is verdict "mismatch".
A verifier clones, runs one command and sends balanced_accuracy as the score.
acceptance.metric: balanced_accuracy - mean of true-positive and true-negative rate, 0 to 1

problems.title: Halve the install footprint of a popular npm package with its tests unchanged
problems.problem:
Install size is paid on every clean CI run by everyone who depends on a package, and it is almost never anybody's job. The usual answers are cheating: drop a feature, move a dependency to peer and let the consumer carry it, or ship less and call it lighter.
Take a package with a real install footprint and a real test suite, and halve the bytes on disk with the public API and the test results unchanged.
This is one of the very few problems here that needs nothing but node, git and a network connection, which is the whole reason it is in the registry.

acceptance.how:
Name in your README a public package, a pinned version and its upstream repo. Your repo runs `make bench`, which installs both arms into clean directories on the same machine in the same run and prints JSON: {megabytes, baseline_megabytes, tests_run, tests_passed, exports_missing}.
tests_run and tests_passed must equal the baseline arm exactly, and exports_missing must be 0: every name the package exported before still has to be there. Either one off, and the verdict is "mismatch" whatever the size says.
A verifier clones, runs one command and sends megabytes as the score.
acceptance.metric: megabytes - bytes on disk after a clean production install, in MB

problems.title: Beat a widely used parser on throughput with byte-identical output
problems.problem:
Most speedups in parsing are bought by being slightly wrong: a fast path that mishandles an escape, a number that loses a digit, an encoding nobody in the test corpus used. The claim is easy to make and hard to check, so it is usually neither.
Pick a widely used parser with a public conformance corpus and beat it on throughput while producing output that is identical byte for byte on every input in that corpus, including the inputs that are supposed to fail.
Identical means identical: same accepted set, same rejected set, same parsed value. A difference on one adversarial input is the whole finding, not a footnote.

acceptance.how:
Name in your README the reference implementation, a pinned version, and a public conformance corpus by URL and commit. Your repo runs `make bench`, which runs both arms over the corpus on the same machine in the same run and prints JSON: {mb_per_second, baseline_mb_per_second, inputs, mismatches}.
mismatches must be 0, counted over accept/reject decisions and over the serialised parsed value. Any non-zero mismatch count is verdict "mismatch", which is the point of the problem rather than an edge case of it.
A verifier clones, runs one command and sends mb_per_second as the score.
acceptance.metric: mb_per_second - input megabytes parsed per second, median of three runs

problems.title: Resolve multi-agent memory conflicts better than last-write-wins
problems.problem: When several agents write into one memory, today's open source stacks settle a clash by recency, by keeping both and sorting it out at read time, or by one LLM judge with a four verb vocabulary. None of them separates a contradiction from a refinement, or from two facts that only look alike. The failure is silent: the store still answers, it just answers with a fact that was superseded, or with one half of a truth it never joined. The author of this problem read the field (Mem0, Zep, Letta, LangMem, Cognee) and found no published calibration and no typed taxonomy. That is their reading, not a checked fact, and it is one of the things a verifier may disagree with.
problems.subject: https://github.com/PJuniszewski/resolver-oss

acceptance.how: Both arms in one run on the same machine. Your repo runs `make bench`, which loads a public labelled conflict corpus (name it and pin the commit in your README) where every pair carries the outcome a careful reader would pick, then runs BOTH the recency baseline (last write wins) and your resolver over that same corpus. Print one JSON line: {accuracy, baseline_accuracy, n, n_contradiction, n_complementary}. The corpus has to hold both kinds and the run has to print their counts, because that is what makes one number honest here: a policy that merges everything scores zero on the complementary pairs, one that keeps everything scores zero on the contradictions, so accuracy over a balanced corpus already refuses both cheats. If n_contradiction or n_complementary is 0, the run is void. A verifier clones, runs one command and sends accuracy.
acceptance.metric: accuracy - fraction of conflicts resolved to the labelled outcome

problems.title: Halve an agent to agent message and keep every qualifier
problems.problem: AXON is a hand designed 31 symbol codec for passing state between agents. Its encoder treats "if", "not", "only" and "all" as filler and drops them, which can reverse the meaning of the sentence it was compressing. The author of this problem measured 24.9% qualifier recall on that repo's own suite; the number is theirs and nobody has repeated it here. The question is older than the repo: compression is scored by how much smaller the text got, the words that carry logic are short, so every ratio driven compressor is under pressure to delete exactly the words that had to survive.
problems.subject: https://github.com/PJuniszewski/axon

acceptance.how: Both arms in one run. Your repo runs `make bench` over a public contrast pair corpus (pin the commit in your README) where each item exists twice, differing only by a logical operator: "deploy if tests pass" against "deploy only if tests pass". The checker has to be mechanical, not a judge. The run compresses each item, asks a receiver model the question that separates the pair, and prints one JSON line: {qualifier_recall, tokens_ratio, uncompressed_recall, n}. tokens_ratio must be 0.5 or lower or the run is void: not compressing is the obvious way to score a perfect recall and it is not an answer. uncompressed_recall comes from the same run and is the ceiling you are being read against.
acceptance.metric: qualifier_recall - fraction of contrast pairs still distinguishable after compression

problems.title: Catch conflicts between parallel agents editing one repository, without flagging everything
problems.problem: When several agents work one repository in parallel, two of them can take decisions that cannot both hold: one moves a call behind a flag, another deletes the flag. Nothing notices, because the files they touched do not overlap, and the merge is clean. ARC compiles a repository into a typed artifact of claims with evidence and offers a merge that flags conflicting decisions across agents. Whether that catches real conflicts is unmeasured, including by its author. The trap sits in the metric: flagging every pair of edits catches all of them.
problems.subject: https://github.com/PJuniszewski/ARC

acceptance.how: Both arms in one run. Your repo runs `make bench` over a public corpus of parallel agent edit sets with labelled conflicts (name it, pin the commit). It runs a file overlap baseline and your detector over the same sets and prints one JSON line: {f1, precision, recall, baseline_f1, n, n_conflicts}. The score is f1, and that is what refuses the flag everything answer, because precision collapses under it. Nothing may execute the repositories under test: this is static analysis of edits, and a run that imports or runs the corpus is void.
acceptance.metric: f1 - harmonic mean of precision and recall on labelled cross agent conflicts

problems.title: Make agent fan out cheaper than one agent, counting every token the fan out spends
problems.problem: Multi agent harnesses fan a task out to subagents and report a reduction in the orchestrator's context. The accounting flatters them twice: it counts the orchestrator's window and not the subagents' own, and it ignores that every spawned agent pays a fixed boot cost, system prompt plus tool schemas, before it does any work at all. The author of this problem measured that boot at roughly 72k tokens per spawn on one harness and concluded fan out is a net loss unless the work per subagent is far larger than it. One harness, one measurement, theirs. This problem asks for the honest version of the claim. No single repository is the subject: the question is about the shape, not about one implementation.

acceptance.how: Both arms in one run on the same machine. Your repo runs `make bench` over a public task suite (pin the commit) and runs BOTH a single agent arm and your fan out arm on every task. Print one JSON line: {total_tokens, solo_total_tokens, solved, solo_solved, n}. total_tokens counts every token every process spent, subagent boot included: the orchestrator's window alone is the wrong denominator and is how this gets reported as a win. solved must be greater than or equal to solo_solved or the run is void, because spending less by doing less is not the result. The score is total_tokens.
acceptance.metric: total_tokens - every token spent by every process, subagent boot included
